newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Short-dated dlr/yen volatilities recoil.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Short-dated dlr/yen volatilities recoil.

text.p: Implied volatilities for shorter-dated dollar/yen options recoiled as spot bounced off overnight lows below 115 yen and stayed in a modest range around 116 yen in U.S. trading, traders said.
Still, the downside strike prices remained bid relative to the upside strikes in the shorter dates after the greenback's four-yen nosedive last Friday, they added.

"It looks frightening like the 110-120 (yen) boundaries are pretty well intact," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. "We've had serious, violent reactions off of both ends of the range."
"We're sitting in the middle of the range...so there will be some reasonable vol pressure," he noted. "But vols can't come off too much, given what we've just seen."

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen fell to 11.7/12.0 percent by late U.S. business from above 12 percent earlier in the day and late on Friday. One-year was also pegged at 11.7/11.9 percent, a touch below Friday's levels.

A Japanese bank trader in New York said traders were reluctant to sell yen calls in the gamma-rich front end, although yen puts were still priced above yen calls in the back end, which tended to be more trend-oriented.

"It's a tough call, but somewhere in the three- to six-month area, they become neutral and gradually flip in favor of yen puts," he said, referring to risk reversals, the put/call pricing differential.
One-month 25-delta risk reversal stood at 0.3/0.5 point in favor of yen calls, little changed from Friday, when a half-point skew for yen puts vanished and reversed as the dollar tumbled.
Dollar/mark volatilities were little changed, despite a bounce in spot. Traders noted that mark volatilities had been little affected on the dollar's way down on Friday either.
"Dollar/mark is a little bit of a different story as this can be, certainly after today's action, perceived more as just a pullback," Revercomb noted.
The dollar, after stalling just short of 1.90 marks last week, tumbled to a low of 1.8383 marks on Friday, but has since clawed back above 1.86 marks today.
Dollar/mark volatility curve was very flat at 11.3/11.5 percent from one-month out to one-year in late trade, marginally off Friday's levels.
Risk reversals still favored the upside strikes, with one-month 25-delta skewed for mark puts by 0.2/0.5 point.
Should spot approach 1.90 marks and threaten to probe higher again, short-covering in the longer-dated mark puts would likely return and buoy back-end volatilities, Revercomb forecast.
"If the dollar resumes the uptrend...you will see a steeper, positive curve," he said.

Still, he added that the dollar proved it would be more violent on a downside break and the U.S. stock and bond markets were still the wild card. T-bond prices seesawed near the lower end of Friday's ranges as the market awaited U.S. retail sales and prices data due out later in the week.
